opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the core problems right now is that there's a big gap between what AI systems can do when you really push on them and what people perceive them as being able to do based on casual interaction. If you're just chatting with a model in a standard interface, with default settings and a modest amount of inference compute, you're seeing something like a lower bound on capabilities. And different people have very different impressions, partly because they're using different setups, different prompts, and different levels of effort.

The idea behind these demonstrations is to try to get closer to an upper bound, or at least a much better estimate of what's actually achievable. That means spending a lot of runtime compute: lots of samples, long agentic rollouts, best-of-n with good selection, careful scaffolding. It also means doing domain-specific elicitation, so actually building tooling and prompting tailored to the task, maybe some fine-tuning, the kind of effort a motivated actor would put in if they really wanted the system to do something.

Why does that help with common knowledge? A few reasons.

First, it's predictive. What you can do today with a huge amount of compute and a lot of elicitation effort tends to be what you'll be able to do cheaply and easily a bit later. Inference costs fall fast, and elicitation techniques get folded into products. So these demonstrations give people a preview, and that's useful for policymakers, labs, and the public who would otherwise be anchored on what they saw six months ago in a chat window.

Second, it's legible. A concrete artifact, like "here's the system autonomously completing this multi-day software engineering task," or "here's it finding this class of vulnerability," is much harder to dismiss than a benchmark number. Benchmarks are useful, but people argue about contamination, about whether the task is representative, and so on. A well-documented demonstration in a domain people care about tends to update people more, and crucially it updates people in a shared way. Everyone can point to the same thing. That's what you want for common knowledge: not just that some individuals know, but that everyone knows that everyone knows.

Third, it reduces the scope for motivated underestimation. If a lab or anyone else says "our model can't really do X," the natural question is how hard they tried. If there's an established practice of serious elicitation, it becomes much harder to sandbag, intentionally or not, and much harder for observers to wave away concerning capabilities as hype.

There are caveats. You have to be thoughtful about which demonstrations you do, because some capabilities, like certain cyber or bio uplift, you don't want to just publish a recipe for. So you might want trusted third parties to run them and report results at an appropriate level of detail. And you need to be careful about the opposite failure, where you cherry-pick and overstate. Good methodology matters: report success rates, cost, how much human help was involved.

But overall I think we're in a world where the most important facts about AI are things like "how close are we to systems that can automate AI research" or "how close are we to dangerous autonomous capabilities," and right now there's a lot of disagreement and confusion about that. Well-run, high-effort demonstrations are one of the better tools we have for turning that into something closer to shared understanding before it really matters.

r001.rationale: The response says demonstrations using substantial compute and elicitation can preview what will become “cheaply and easily” available as inference costs fall and techniques enter products.

r002.rationale: It hopes to build shared understanding “before it really matters,” but does not clearly say this will happen before the capability is widely used.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underrated things that could happen in the next few years. The basic issue is that when people look at AI capabilities, they're usually looking at the sort of default thing: you type a question into a chat interface, you get an answer back in 30 seconds, and you form an impression from that. And that impression is often quite far from what the model is actually capable of if you're willing to spend a lot more on it.

So concretely, what I mean by very high runtime compute is something like: instead of spending a few cents on a query, you spend thousands or tens of thousands of dollars. You let the model run for days, you have it try the problem many, many times in parallel, you have it check its own work, build up intermediate results, and so on. And then domain-specific elicitation is the other piece, which is that you have people who actually know the domain, who know what the model is bad at, build scaffolding and prompts and tools that are specifically designed to get the most out of it on that class of problem. And the combination of those two things often gets you a wildly different picture of the capability level than what you'd see from casual use.

I think the reason this matters for common knowledge is that right now there's a lot of disagreement about where things are, and some of that disagreement is just people looking at different evidence. Someone who's spent a bunch of time with heavily elicited systems on hard problems has a different model than someone who's seen the thing fail at something that seemed easy. And if you could have a demonstration that was sort of legible and hard to argue with, like "here's a problem that experts in this field agree is actually hard, here's what we spent, and here's what came out," then I think that would help pull people's views together. Not necessarily toward alarm, but toward actually agreeing on the facts.

There's also a forecasting angle here, which I think is important. If a capability is achievable today with, say, a hundred thousand dollars of compute and a bunch of careful elicitation, then historically that capability has tended to become cheap and default within a year or two, as the models improve and the elicitation gets baked in. So the expensive demonstration is kind of a preview of what the cheap version looks like soon. And that's a very useful thing for policymakers and labs to have, because it gives you lead time. You're not just saying "trust me, this is coming," you're saying "here it is, it's just expensive right now."

I'll say there are a couple of caveats. One is that it's easy to do this badly. If the demonstration is cherry-picked or the problem turns out to have been in the training data or whatever, then you've actually made things worse, because now the skeptics have a legitimate reason to dismiss the whole genre. So I'd want these to be done carefully, with external verification, with people who are motivated to poke holes in it. And the other caveat is that there's some tension with the fact that a lot of the most informative demonstrations would be in dangerous domains, like bio or cyber, and you obviously don't want to publish detailed results there. But I think there's still a lot of room for demonstrations on things like math or software engineering or scientific research tasks that are hard, legible, and don't have those problems.

So overall I'm fairly bullish on it. I think it's one of the cheaper interventions, relatively speaking, for improving the quality of the collective conversation about where we are.

r001.rationale: The response says a capability demonstrated with high compute and careful elicitation can become “cheap and default within a year or two.”

r002.rationale: It says an expensive demonstration can pull views together and give policymakers and labs lead time before the capability becomes cheap and default.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic idea is that there can be a pretty big gap between what a model can do in a normal interaction and what it can do if you put a lot of effort into getting good performance on a particular task. You might give it much more time to work, let it try lots of approaches, and build scaffolding that’s specifically suited to that domain.

A demonstration like that could make a capability much harder to dismiss. Instead of arguing about whether a model’s benchmark score implies that it could do some economically important work, you can show it actually doing that work. And if the demonstration is public and credible, people can also see that other people have seen it. That’s part of what gets you from a capability being known by a few researchers to something closer to common knowledge.

I’d distinguish that from showing that the capability is cheap or reliable enough to deploy widely. If you spend an enormous amount of compute on one successful attempt, that establishes something different from doing the task consistently at a competitive cost. You’d want to be clear about the resources involved, how much human help there was, and how the task was selected.

But even an expensive demonstration can be useful. It can establish that a capability is already attainable under some conditions, rather than leaving the discussion entirely dependent on predictions about future systems.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts an expensive demonstration with capability that is cheap and reliable enough for wide deployment, but does not anticipate that the capability may soon stop requiring high runtime compute or domain-specific elicitation.

r002.rationale: It says a public, credible demonstration can move a capability toward common knowledge, while distinguishing that from being cheap or reliable enough for wide deployment. This communicates that common knowledge can be established before widespread use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing you can do is take a capability where people disagree about whether the model can actually do it, and make a pretty serious effort to elicit it. Give it a lot of runtime compute, build scaffolding for that particular domain, and have people who understand the domain work on getting good performance. Then demonstrate the result in a way that other people can inspect and ideally reproduce.

That can help distinguish “the model can’t do this” from “the model doesn’t do this when you ask it a question in a chat interface.” Those are potentially very different claims. And if you get a convincing demonstration, people can update not just on the capability, but on the fact that other people have seen evidence of the capability too. That’s the common-knowledge aspect.

There are some important qualifications. If you spend an enormous amount of compute, you haven’t necessarily shown that the capability is economically useful at current prices. And you need to be clear about how much assistance the humans provided, whether you selected the best result out of lots of attempts, and how reliable the whole process is. But even an expensive demonstration can establish that a capability is available under some conditions, which can be quite relevant for thinking about risks.

I’d also be more confident interpreting success than failure here. If a serious elicitation effort succeeds, that tells you something fairly concrete. If it fails, it’s harder to know whether the model lacks the capability or whether you just haven’t found the right way to get it to do the task.

r001.rationale: The response describes an expensive demonstration and distinguishes it from economic usefulness at current prices, but does not anticipate that the compute or elicitation requirements may soon disappear.

r002.rationale: The response explains how a demonstration could establish common knowledge, but does not say this would happen before the capability is widely used.
